# Introduction

I want to determine a humbly-optimized strategy for my long-term investment portfolio. My goal is to maximize the [utility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility) I will derive from this portfolio. Assuming constant relative risk aversion and a utility function of the following form, as per [Merton's portfolio problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merton's_portfolio_problem):

$$
u(x) = \frac{x^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}
$$

where

- $u(x)$ is the utility derived from an $x$ level of wealth (which is consumed to produce utility)
- $x$ is the amount of wealth consumed
- and $\gamma$ is a constant measuring the level of risk aversion

I estimated that, personally, $\gamma = 2$. This estimation is out of the scope of this study, see Haghani & White ([2018](https://elmwealth.com/measuring-the-fabric-of-felicity/)) for an introduction.

@fig-crra-utility shows the shape of my utility function: utility rises with consumed wealth but with decreasing marginal return, and $\gamma$ sets how fast that marginal rate of return decays.

```{python}
#| label: fig-crra-utility
#| fig-cap: "CRRA utility of consumed wealth, for my $\\gamma = 2$ and two other risk aversion levels, for comparison. (Utility is ordinal, only the shape of the curve is meaningful, not the absolute values. And values cannot be compared across distinct functions like the three above.)"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0.5, 5, 400)
crra_gammas = [(1.5, "#E69F00", 1.2), (2.0, "#0072B2", 2.2), (3.0, "#009E73", 1.2)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for gamma, color, linewidth in crra_gammas:
    ax.plot(
        x,
        x ** (1 - gamma) / (1 - gamma),
        color=color,
        linewidth=linewidth,
        label=f"γ = {gamma:g}",
    )
ax.set_xlim(x.min(), x.max())
ax.set_ylim(-3, 0.15)
ax.set_xlabel("Wealth consumed, x")
ax.set_ylabel("Utility, u(x)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=3, loc="lower right")
ax.grid(True, axis="y", color="0.92")
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

I am designing this strategy to be implemented in an [Interactive Brokers (IBKR) *compte-titre ordinaire* (CTO)](https://www.interactivebrokers.ie/en/accounts/individual.php?menu=B) as a French citizen. This broker and this type of account give access to a wide array of instruments and services.

I have already defined the universe of assets I will consider and submit to the optimization (all EUR-denominated):

- an [MSCI ACWI](https://www.msci.com/indexes/index/892400/msci-acwi-index) ETF such as [IUSQ](https://www.justetf.com/en/etf-profile.html?isin=IE00B6R52259) (0.20 % TER);
- a EUR-hedged US Treasury 7-10 year bond ETF such as [CEMF](https://www.justetf.com/en/etf-profile.html?isin=IE000K1VI152) or [7USH](https://www.justetf.com/en/etf-profile.html?isin=LU1407888137) (0.10 & 0.06 % TER, respectively);
- a [managed futures](https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Research/White-Papers/Understanding-Managed-Futures) ETF such as [DBMFE](https://www.imgp.com/fund/LU2951555403-imgp-dbi-managed-futures-fund-r-eur-ucits-etf/) (0.75 % TER) (ideally, several ones to diversify the manager risk);
- and a gold ETF -- [PPFB](https://www.justetf.com/en/etf-profile.html?isin=IE00B4ND3602) (0.12 % TER).

The definition of this universe is out of scope but was inspired, among others, by Ilmanen ([2022](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/shop/general-finance-investments/investing-amid-low-expected-returns-making-the-most-when-markets-offer-the-least-p-9781119860198)).

An IBKR CTO allows the implementation of short box spreads for fixed-rate, low-cost leverage. The derivation of the properties of this combination of options is fascinating but also kept out of the scope of this study, see [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_spread).

Analytical process:

- I will first define the inputs of the optimizer -- the assets' expected return, volatility and correlation. The rest of the analysis is extremely sensitive to those inputs, hence, I will employ techniques designed to keep them as humble and evidence-based as possible.
- I will then run mean-variance optimization (MVO) on those inputs to identify the [tangency portfolio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_portfolio_theory#Tangency_portfolio), as per the modern portfolio theory.
- I will then solve for the amount of leverage to apply to this optimized portfolio to maximize utility. In summary, the challenge so far consists in (i) estimating the portfolio of assets that will maximize the expected return per unit of risk taken, and then (ii) leverage it to the level of risk that best suits my psychology (@eq-challenge).

$$
\underbrace{\frac{\text{return}}{\text{risk}}}_{\text{to maximize}} \times \underbrace{\text{leverage}}_{\substack{\text{to adapt to my} \\ \text{risk aversion level}}}
$$ {#eq-challenge}

- Finally, I will stress test the levered portfolio out of sample, regarding the risk of forced liquidation^[IBKR does not use margin calls, they liquidate directly.].


# Historical returns

Historical returns are important (but not sufficient) factors in the determination of the MVO inputs. They are estimated from long-history proxies of the actual ETFs I would invest in because those ETFs are too recent. Return time series are monthly and denominated in EUR.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import sys

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# The study's Python modules live in src/.
sys.path.insert(0, "src")

from data import hedge_tracking_check, monthly_returns_matrix
from mu import BOX_REAL


def mask_upper(matrix):
    """Blank the strictly-upper-triangular cells for displaying a symmetric matrix."""
    keep = np.tril(np.ones(matrix.shape, dtype=bool))
    return matrix.where(keep, "")


returns = monthly_returns_matrix()

# Study window and size, surfaced in the prose below.
data_start = f"{returns.index.min():%Y-%m}"
data_end = f"{returns.index.max():%Y-%m}"
n_months = len(returns)
n_years = round(n_months / 12)
box_fmt = f"{BOX_REAL:.2%}"  # real box borrowing rate R_B, reused across the prose

# EUR-hedge reconstruction vs the live hedged ETFs, surfaced in the prose below.
_hedge = hedge_tracking_check()
hedge_7ush_n = int(_hedge.loc["7USH", "months"])
hedge_7ush_from = _hedge.loc["7USH", "from"]
hedge_7ush_corr = f"{_hedge.loc['7USH', 'correlation']:.2f}"
hedge_7ush_diff = f"{_hedge.loc['7USH', 'difference (bp/y)']:+.0f}"
```

I had to reconstruct the EUR hedging component of my bonds sleeve proxy data. My target vehicle is a EUR-hedged UCITS ETF on the ICE US Treasury 7-10 y index, but this type of instrument is too recent for a long study, so I (i) proxy the underlying with [IEF](https://www.ishares.com/us/products/239456/ishares-710-year-treasury-bond-etf) -- a US ETF on the same index -- and (ii) simulate the EUR hedge. Hedging is simulated by assuming a rolling one-month currency forward contract was held on the index's full market value, as per [ICE Bond Index Methodologies](https://www.ice.com/publicdocs/data/Bond_Index_Methodologies.pdf), pp. 22-23; I don't have that forward series, but [covered interest parity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interest_rate_parity) ties its cost to the short-rate differential between the two legs of the currency forward (EUR & USD), so I add the one-month carry from [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS1MO) short rates (the euro overnight rate (`IRSTCI01EZM156N`) minus the 1-month US T-bill (`DGS1MO`)). Against [7USH](https://www.justetf.com/en/etf-profile.html?isin=LU1407888137), over the `{python} hedge_7ush_n` months from `{python} hedge_7ush_from`, the correlation is `{python} hedge_7ush_corr` and my reconstructed proxy data differs from 7USH's annualized return by only `{python} hedge_7ush_diff` bp/yr. But that validation only reaches back to 2023.

The SG CTA Index is the live, net-of-fee return of a [pool of the largest managed-futures CTAs](https://wholesale.banking.societegenerale.com/fileadmin/indices_feeds/SG_CTA_Index_Constituents.pdf). It is a good proxy for DBMFE (which uses it as its benchmark). DBMFE is an unhedged, EUR-denominated share class, so I simply convert the USD index to EUR and leave it unhedged.

The resulting cross-sectionally-complete time frame is `{python} data_start` to `{python} data_end` (~`{python} n_years` years, `{python} n_months` months). It spans the tail of the dot-com bear, the GFC, the Covid crisis, and the 2022 inflationary crisis & stock–bond correlation sign flip.

# Computing the inputs of the mean-variance optimizer
## Covariance matrix
### Historical covariances & Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage

```{python}
#| label: ledoit-wolf
import numpy as np

from covariance import ledoit_wolf_covariance, correlation

cov_lw, delta = ledoit_wolf_covariance(returns)
lw_delta_fmt = f"{delta:.2f}"

# Shrinkage target: the average of the off-diagonal sample correlations.
sample_corr = returns.corr()
off_diagonal = ~np.eye(len(sample_corr), dtype=bool)
avg_corr_fmt = f"{sample_corr.values[off_diagonal].mean():.2f}"
```

The sample of historical returns allows us to compute a covariance matrix. But, as per Ledoit & Wolf ([2003](http://www.ledoit.net/honey.pdf)), "nobody should be using the sample covariance matrix for the purpose of portfolio optimization" because of its estimation error. As such, our sample covariance matrix is shrunk toward a constant-correlation target with the optimal shrinkage constant $\delta$ set to `{python} lw_delta_fmt` by the Ledoit-Wolf estimator^[The problem targeted by Ledoit & Wolf is most important in cases where the number of assets surpasses the number of observations in each return time series which is far from our case, but I apply that method for robustness.]. That results in each pair-wise correlation coefficient being pulled toward the average sample pair-wise correlation coefficient (@tbl-shrinkage).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-shrinkage
#| tbl-cap: "Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk correlations; each off-diagonal cell shows the shrunk value, with the shift from the sample correlation in parentheses."
_shrunk = correlation(cov_lw)
_shift = _shrunk - returns.corr()
_cells = _shrunk.copy().astype(object)
for _i in _shrunk.index:
    for _j in _shrunk.columns:
        _cells.loc[_i, _j] = (
            "1.00"
            if _i == _j
            else f"{_shrunk.loc[_i, _j]:.2f} ({round(_shift.loc[_i, _j], 2) + 0.0:+.2f})"
        )
mask_upper(_cells)
```

The shifts shown in parentheses in @tbl-shrinkage are small, so the pull toward the `{python} avg_corr_fmt` average correlation is mild.


### Regime inspection

The correlations above -- sample or shrunk -- are full-period averages.
They hide the evolution of the degree of comovement over time between the sleeve proxies.
I want equities to be anticorrelated to the other sleeves when equities crash. An average correlation doesn't provide enough time granularity to examine this.
So it is important that we scrutinize those single numbers before feeding them to MVO. In @tbl-regime-corr, I bucket the `{python} n_months` months of data by the sign of their equity return and compute each sleeve's correlation with equity within each bucket.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-regime-corr
#| tbl-cap: "Correlation with equity by equity-state bucket."
from regimes import conditional_correlations

cc = conditional_correlations(returns)
trend_up_fmt = f"{cc.loc['equity up', 'trend']:.2f}"
trend_down_fmt = f"{cc.loc['equity down', 'trend']:.2f}"
trend_worst_fmt = f"{cc.loc['equity worst quartile', 'trend']:.2f}"
gold_worst_fmt = f"{cc.loc['equity worst quartile', 'gold']:.2f}"

(
    cc.rename_axis("equity state")
    .reset_index()
    .style.hide(axis="index")
    .format(precision=2)
)
```

@tbl-regime-corr shows that:

- Bonds acted as a risk-off hedge: negatively correlated with equity throughout, and increasingly so as equity weakens -- deepest in its worst quartile (@tbl-regime-corr).
- Trend acted as a convex hedge: mildly positively-correlated with equity when equity rises (`{python} trend_up_fmt`), but turning slightly negatively-correlated when equity falls (`{python} trend_down_fmt` to `{python} trend_worst_fmt`).
- Gold acted as a tail hedge: roughly uncorrelated when equity rises or falls modestly, but negatively-correlated (`{python} gold_worst_fmt`) in the worst quartile.

The buckets in @tbl-regime-corr pool months regardless of when they occurred. @fig-rolling-corr instead shows how equity correlated with the other sleeves over time.

@fig-rolling-corr provides additional insights:

- As the [headlines](https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Perspectives/A-Positive-Stock-Bond-Correlation-Is-a-Terrible-Reason-to-Add-More-Equity-Risk-to-Your-Portfolio) said, the stock-bond correlation turned positive. Negative for most of the period, it flipped sign around 2022 and remained elevated into 2025 (@fig-rolling-corr). The risk-off hedge of the 2000s and 2010s has, for now, become a risk-on co-mover.
- Trend's correlation to stocks swings widely (from +0.76 in 2006 to -0.35 in 2024), consistent with its convex, regime-dependent behavior.
- And gold's was most stable (-0.33 to +0.39), albeit rarely substantially anticorrelated.


### The final covariance

The regime inspection highlights one correlation to scrutinize: the equity-bonds one. Our EUR-hedged US Treasury sleeve yields a genuinely negative correlation to equity, most times. That's a flight-to-quality phenomenon which is the main property this instrument was chosen for (@tbl-regime-corr): it rallied while equities fell through the GFC and Covid. It is not an all-weather hedge, though: the correlation turned positive since the 2022 inflationary crisis and both our equities & bonds sleeves crashed together. The rolling correlation was still high at the end of the sample period (@fig-rolling-corr).

But I do not treat that negative sample correlation as a forward constant. Its sign is regime-dependent: negative during deflationary shocks, positive during inflationary crises (Campbell, Sunderam & Viceira, [2009](https://www.nber.org/papers/w14701)). The 2022 flip demonstrates the latter case. Forward-looking capital-market assumptions place the equity-bonds correlation near zero and regime-unstable rather than reliably negative -- J.P. Morgan's [2026 LTCMA](https://am.jpmorgan.com/us/en/asset-management/institutional/insights/portfolio-insights/ltcma/) assumes ~0.02 for US equities versus Treasuries, Amundi treats cross-asset correlations as unstable ([2026](https://research-center.amundi.com/article/capital-market-assumptions-2026)), and PIMCO ([2024](https://www.pimco.com/us/en/insights/negative-correlations-positive-allocations)) finds it turns negative only when inflation sits near central-bank targets (i.e., when unexpected inflation is low). Therefore, I override the equity-bonds correlation to 0 (@tbl-final-corr). Bonds' inflation-regime blind spot is left for gold and trend following to manage.

The non-equity sleeves' crisis-hedging value is convex and state-dependent, which is an information a single covariance matrix cannot convey. Editing the correlations cannot capture it. MVO prices these sleeves on their average comovement, so it under-weights the tail protection they offer. This is a known limitation of any single-covariance optimizer, which I accept.

What MVO is fed is the covariance matrix $\Sigma$: its diagonal holds the sleeve variances (the volatilities squared) and its off-diagonal entries are the covariances ($\Sigma_{ij} = \sigma_i\,\sigma_j\,\rho_{ij}$). @tbl-final-corr and @tbl-final-vol decompose it into correlations and volatilities for legibility.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-final-corr
#| tbl-cap: "Final correlation matrix (Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk; equity-bonds correlation overridden to 0)."
from covariance import annualized_vols, final_covariance

cov_final = final_covariance(returns, rho_equity_bonds=0.0)
mask_upper(correlation(cov_final).map("{:.2f}".format))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-final-vol
#| tbl-cap: "Final annualized volatilities (sample; no override)."
(
    pd.DataFrame({"annualized vol": annualized_vols(cov_final).map("{:.1%}".format)})
    .rename_axis("sleeve")
    .reset_index()
    .style.hide(axis="index")
)
```


## Expected returns

The second MVO input is the vector of expected returns -- the least reliable estimates, and one of the inputs MVO is most sensitive to. So, rather than feeding my own point estimates directly, I pass them through a Black-Litterman model (He & Litterman, [1999](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=334304); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black%E2%80%93Litterman_model)): it starts with the market-implied returns (more on that below), considered as a reasonable anchor (playing the role of a Bayesian prior), and tilts them toward my personal views using a given confidence level I also provide.


### The equilibrium prior

The market-implied return is the equilibrium return of the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM; Sharpe, [1964](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1964.tb02865.x)), recovered by reverse optimization. A mean-variance investor with risk-aversion coefficient $\gamma_M$ (the market's risk aversion, distinct from my own CRRA $\gamma$; $\lambda$ in Idzorek's notation) chooses risky-asset weights $w$ to maximize the quadratic utility $U(w) = w'\Pi - \tfrac{\gamma_M}{2}\,w'\Sigma w$, where $\Pi$ is the vector of expected excess returns over the risk-free rate and $\Sigma$ their covariance matrix. Its first-order condition, $\Pi - \gamma_M\Sigma w = 0$, gives the optimal weights $w = \tfrac{1}{\gamma_M}\Sigma^{-1}\Pi$ (Markowitz, [1952](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1952.tb01525.x)). Reverse optimization inverts this relation: taking the capitalization-weighted market portfolio $w_\text{mkt}$ as optimal, the excess returns that justify holding it are

$$
\Pi = \gamma_M\,\Sigma\,w_\text{mkt}
$$

the implied equilibrium returns (Idzorek, [2007](https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-075068321-0.50003-0)), where $w_\text{mkt}$ is the vector of market-capitalization weights. Adding the risk-free rate gives the expected return reported in @tbl-bl-prior.

The weights $w_\text{mkt}$ are the market capitalizations normalized to sum to one, which treats the four sleeves as the whole market. They are not -- credit, real estate, cash and many other assets are excluded -- but computing the equilibrium over the investable universe rather than a literally global market portfolio is the standard Black-Litterman construction, in which the market is the set of assets under consideration (He & Litterman, [1999](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=334304); Idzorek, [2007](https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-075068321-0.50003-0)). The prior is thus the CAPM-implied return within that universe. @tbl-bl-prior shows the capitalizations (in USD for data availability but only the ratios matter, so the currency is irrelevant), the implied weights, and the prior:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bl-prior
#| tbl-cap: "Market capitalizations, the implied market weights, and the equilibrium prior Π (real)."
import black_litterman as bl
from black_litterman import MARKET_CAPS, market_weights
from mu import RF_REAL

bl_prior = bl.equilibrium_prior(cov_final)
bl_delta = bl.market_delta(cov_final)
bl_delta_fmt = f"{bl_delta:.1f}"
cap_equity_fmt = f"{MARKET_CAPS['equity']:.0f}"
cap_bonds_fmt = f"{MARKET_CAPS['bonds']:.0f}"
cap_gold_fmt = f"{MARKET_CAPS['gold']:.0f}"
eq_mktwt_fmt = f"{market_weights(cov_final.index)['equity']:.0%}"
trend_vol = cov_final.loc["trend", "trend"] ** 0.5
trend_sharpe = 0.2  # forward net Sharpe assigned to the trend sleeve
trend_sharpe_fmt = f"{trend_sharpe:.1f}"
trend_vol_fmt = f"{trend_vol:.1%}"
rf_real_fmt = f"{RF_REAL:.2%}"
trend_excess_fmt = f"{trend_sharpe * trend_vol:.1%}"
trend_return_fmt = f"{trend_sharpe * trend_vol + RF_REAL:.1%}"
_caps = pd.Series(MARKET_CAPS).reindex(cov_final.index)
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "capitalization (USD trillion)": _caps.map(lambda x: "--" if pd.isna(x) else f"{x:,.1f}"),
        "market weight": market_weights(cov_final.index).map("{:.1%}".format),
        "prior Π": bl_prior.map("{:.2%}".format),
    }
).rename_axis("sleeve").reset_index().style.hide(axis="index")
```

The capitalizations are the MSCI ACWI free-float market cap (\$`{python} cap_equity_fmt` tn, [MSCI factsheet](https://www.msci.com/documents/10199/255599/msci-acwi-net.pdf), 2026), the US Treasury notes and bonds outstanding (\$`{python} cap_bonds_fmt` tn, [FiscalData MSPD](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/monthly-statement-public-debt/summary-of-treasury-securities-outstanding), 2026-07), and WGC financial gold (\$`{python} cap_gold_fmt` tn, [WGC](https://www.gold.org/goldhub/research/market-primer/gold-market-primer-market-size-and-structure), 2026). Managed futures don't have a market capitalization, so they take weight $0$ in the market portfolio. Their equilibrium prior is still not exactly zero, though: the market-implied return depends on each asset's covariance with the market (its $\beta$) rather than on its own weight, and managed futures' low $\beta$ puts them at near-zero prior. Their return therefore comes almost entirely from the view.

The market's risk aversion, $\gamma_M$, is needed, in this process, to scale the prior $\Pi$ (and, downstream, the leverage). It is computed based on a set of professional equity risk premium (ERP) assumptions: I set $\gamma_M$ so that the market-implied return on equity equals that premium, $\gamma_M = \text{ERP} / \operatorname{cov}(\text{equity}, \text{market})$, and every other sleeve's implied return then follows from its covariance with the market. Equity is ~`{python} eq_mktwt_fmt` of the market and the only sleeve with a well-identified premium, so anchoring $\gamma_M$ to it keeps every input sourced. The ERP is an external number, not my view on equity. The forward-looking estimates cluster near 5 %: [Damodaran](https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/datafile/histimpl.html) (implied US, 4.23 %), [Kroll](https://www.kroll.com/en/reports/cost-of-capital/recommended-us-equity-risk-premium-and-corresponding-risk-free-rates) (US, 5.0 %), and the [Fernandez 2026 survey](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6570342) (5.5 %), averaging ~4.9 %; the [DMS/UBS 2026 Yearbook](https://www.ubs.com/content/dam/assets/wm/static/cio/documents/giry2026-summary-public.pdf) anchors the magnitude with the long-run realized premium over bills (US equities 6.6 % vs bills 0.5 %, real, 1900-2025; lower for the world). I take 5.0 % as an arbitrary center point in that range. We land on $\gamma_M \approx$ `{python} bl_delta_fmt`.


### My views

Each sleeve's view is an estimate (partly inspired by Ilmanen's ([2022](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/shop/general-finance-investments/investing-amid-low-expected-returns-making-the-most-when-markets-offer-the-least-p-9781119860198)) asset class-specific methods) fed to the Black-Litterman model with a confidence level (between 0 and 1) representing my degree of trust in the estimate (Idzorek, [2007](https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-075068321-0.50003-0)):

- **Bonds: ~1.3 % real, confidence 0.7.** The ICE US Treasury 7-10 y index the sleeve tracks yields 4.54 % to maturity (nominal, USD, and gross of fees by construction; [CEMF](https://www.ishares.com/uk/individual/en/products/344759/ishares-treasury-bond-7-10yr-ucits-etf), 2026-08-25). Because it is a constant-maturity index -- it rolls down the curve rather than holding to maturity -- the forward-looking return is carry plus roll-down, not the yield alone (Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen & Vrugt, [2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2017.11.002)): the 7-10 y segment slopes at ~5 bp/y ([FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS10), `DGS10` 4.70 % against `DGS7` 4.55 %, 2026-08-24), which over the index's 6.83-year effective duration is worth ~0.34 pp. That is a claim on the term premium rather than free carry: under the expectations hypothesis an upward-sloping curve implies short rates rise by just enough to cancel the roll-down, so I keep the 0.34 pp only because the 7-10 y term premium is positive and comfortably wider than what I am claiming. Hedging to EUR gives up the USD-minus-EUR short-rate differential (covered interest parity) -- currently ~1.60 pp (US 1-month 3.79 %, [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS1MO), 2026-08-24; €STR 2.189 %, [ECB](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/financial_markets_and_interest_rates/euro_short-term_rate/html/index.en.html), 2026-08-25). I charge no cross-currency basis on top of that. The mechanism is real and has persisted since 2008 (Du, Tepper & Verdelhan, [2018](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12620)), but it is doesn't seem material today: CME's [XEURBI](https://www.cmegroup.com/market-data/cme-group-benchmark-administration/eur-usd-cross-currency-basis-index.html) index put the EUR/USD basis between +0.02 and -0.60 bp over 2026-08-20 to 08-26, against -35 to -45 bp in 2023. That leaves ~3.28 % hedged nominal; minus ~2 % expected inflation ([ECB SPF](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/ecb_surveys/survey_of_professional_forecasters/html/ecb.spf2026q3.en.html)) gives ~1.28 % real. My confidence level is high despite this intricate estimation gymnastic because the starting yield is a strong forward predictor of the nominal return, while the CAPM prior is a weak model for bonds.
- **Equity: 4.03 % real, confidence 0.8.** Elm Wealth's all-world payout-adjusted cyclically-adjusted earnings yield (P-CAEY; White & Haghani, [2024](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4874559)) -- a direct forward real-return estimate -- at 4.03 % ([Elm Wealth](https://elmwealth.com/capital-market-assumptions/), 2026-07-27). It is forward-facing and valuation-aware, whereas the prior is valuation-blind.
- **Trend: ~2.7 % real, confidence 0.65.** A lot of evidence backs the trend premium. It was positive over every decade since 1800 (Lempérière et al., [2014](https://doi.org/10.21314/JOIS.2014.043)), a diversified time-series-momentum Sharpe above 1 since 1966 (Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen, [2012](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2011.11.003)), and robust across a century net of fees (Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen, [2017](https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2017.44.1.015)). Its existence is well-established. Its magnitude is not, though. Those studies' gross Sharpes of 0.7 to >1 come from stronger, less-crowded pre-2000 trends, while the live net-of-fee DBMFE I proxy with the SG CTA Index had a Sharpe of only ~0.13 over our sample period. I place my view between those bounds. The EUR-unhedged SG CTA that DBMFE benchmarks carries a ~`{python} trend_vol_fmt` volatility; I assign it a forward net Sharpe of `{python} trend_sharpe_fmt`. Its excess real return is then `{python} trend_sharpe_fmt` $\times$ `{python} trend_vol_fmt` $\approx$ `{python} trend_excess_fmt`, and adding the `{python} rf_real_fmt` real risk-free cash rate (the collateral yield $R_F$, not the box borrowing rate; cf. @sec-leverage) gives `{python} trend_return_fmt` real. The confidence is set below the ones of equity and bonds, and above what a noisy estimate would get, because the CAPM equilibrium prior is structurally unfit here: trend is an anomaly a single-factor model cannot price correctly which penalizes managed futures given their low beta.
- **Gold: no view.** No cashflow and no forward anchor (long-run real return $\approx$ inflation according to Ilmanen ([2022](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/shop/general-finance-investments/investing-amid-low-expected-returns-making-the-most-when-markets-offer-the-least-p-9781119860198))), so I express nothing and leave gold at its equilibrium prior.


### The posterior {#sec-posterior}

The Black-Litterman model blends each view with the prior in inverse proportion to their uncertainties (Idzorek's confidence method, $\tau = 0.05$^[$\tau$ scales the prior's uncertainty level. A small $\tau$ makes the prior harder to depart from. 0.05 is the conventional value.]):

I would hold each sleeve via an ETF a vehicle that charges fees. I deduct them here, from the posterior, rather than earlier from the views because a fee is not a belief about the market. The trend proxy data is already net of fees.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bl-posterior
#| tbl-cap: "Black-Litterman prior, view, confidence, and posterior μ, before and after the vehicle's ongoing charge (real)."
from black_litterman import VIEW_CONFIDENCES, vehicle_fees
from mu import VIEWS_REAL

bl_post = bl.posterior_returns(cov_final)
bl_net = bl.posterior_net_returns(cov_final)
_ters = vehicle_fees(cov_final.index)
_rows = {}
for _a in cov_final.index:
    _has_view = _a in VIEW_CONFIDENCES
    _rows[_a] = {
        "prior Π": f"{bl_prior[_a]:.2%}",
        "view": f"{VIEWS_REAL[_a]:.2%}" if _has_view else "--",
        "confidence": f"{VIEW_CONFIDENCES[_a]:.1f}" if _has_view else "--",
        "posterior μ": f"{bl_post[_a]:.2%}",
        "TER": f"{_ters[_a]:.2%}",
        "net μ": f"{bl_net[_a]:.2%}",
    }
pd.DataFrame(_rows).T.rename_axis("sleeve").reset_index().style.hide(axis="index")
```

This posterior is the MVO input. The posterior equity return is not far from my view; bonds also are only modestly shrunk; trend is pulled part-way down from 2.7 % toward its near-zero prior; and gold, though it carries no view, is still pulled above its prior by its covariance with the viewed sleeves.


# Determining the portfolio weights

MVO is fed the posterior $\mu$ (@tbl-bl-posterior) and the covariance $\Sigma$, and outputs the weights of the max-Sharpe portfolio, also called the [tangency portfolio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_portfolio_theory#Tangency_portfolio) (@tbl-tangency). Considering that lending & borrowing do not occur at the same insterest rates ($R_F$ & $R_B$, respectively) and that I'll be borrowing, not lending, the [two-fund separation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_fund_separation_theorem) applies using $R_B$. So I feed MVO $R_B$ and lever up the resulting tangency portfolio to my risk aversion level (next section; remember @eq-challenge?).

@tbl-mvo-inputs shows what the optimizer sees per sleeve next to the resulting weights.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-mvo-inputs
#| tbl-cap: "What MVO sees per sleeve: net posterior return, volatility, Sharpe, and correlation with equity, next to the resulting tangency weight (real, considering the borrowing rate $R_B$)."
from composition import tangency_weights
from mu import BOX_REAL

_vols = annualized_vols(cov_final)
_w = tangency_weights(cov_final, bl_net, rf=BOX_REAL)
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "net μ": bl_net.map("{:.2%}".format),
        "excess (μ - R_B)": (bl_net - BOX_REAL).map("{:.2%}".format),
        "ann. vol. σ": _vols.map("{:.1%}".format),
        "Sharpe": ((bl_net - BOX_REAL) / _vols).map("{:.2f}".format),
        "corr w/ equity": correlation(cov_final)["equity"].map("{:.2f}".format),
        "tangency weight": _w.map("{:.1%}".format),
    }
).rename_axis("sleeve").reset_index().style.hide(axis="index")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-tangency
#| tbl-cap: "The tangency portfolio: max-Sharpe of the Black-Litterman model's posterior returns and of the covariance matrix (real, considering the borrowing rate $R_B$)."
from composition import portfolio_performance, tangency_weights
from mu import BOX_REAL

w_risky = tangency_weights(cov_final, bl_net, rf=BOX_REAL)
r_risky, s_risky, sh_risky = portfolio_performance(w_risky, bl_net, cov_final, rf=BOX_REAL)
_row = {f"{sleeve} weight": f"{weight:.1%}" for sleeve, weight in w_risky.items()}
_row.update({"E[r]": f"{r_risky:.1%}", "σ": f"{s_risky:.1%}", "Sharpe": f"{sh_risky:.2f}"})
tang_vol_fmt = f"{s_risky:.0%}"
w_equity_fmt = f"{w_risky['equity']:.0%}"
w_bonds_fmt = f"{w_risky['bonds']:.0%}"
w_trend_fmt = f"{w_risky['trend']:.0%}"
w_gold_fmt = f"{w_risky['gold']:.0%}"
pd.DataFrame([_row]).style.hide(axis="index")
```


# Applying leverage {#sec-leverage}

The tangency portfolio's volatility (~`{python} tang_vol_fmt`) is far below the risk level I should bear, given its Sharpe, to maximize utility, so I borrow to lever it up. I finance that borrowing with short box spreads at $R_B \approx$ `{python} box_fmt` real -- 3-month Euribor (2.524 %, [2026-08-21](https://www.euribor-rates.eu/en/current-euribor-rates/2/euribor-rate-3-months/)) plus 0.3 pp -- a realistic EUR box execution premium ([Cayas](https://cayas.fr/le-journal/msci-world-assurance-vie-pilotee-allocation-cayas-meilleure) considers Euribor 3M + 0.1 to 0.5 pp) -- minus ~2 % expected inflation.

The optimal leverage ratio is solved the [Merton portfolio problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merton's_portfolio_problem). For the CRRA utility of the introduction, a single risky asset of expected return $\mu$ and volatility $\sigma$, and lending/borrowing at a risk-free rate $r$, Merton's solution is a constant optimal fraction of wealth in the risky asset,

$$
w^* = \frac{\mu - r}{\gamma\,\sigma^2}
$$

My risky asset is the tangency portfolio presented earlier -- expected return $\mu_p$, volatility $\sigma$ -- and I borrow to lever it at the box rate $R_B$, so its optimal weight is as follows (just by remapping the variables)

$$
k^* = \frac{\mu_p - R_B}{\gamma\,\sigma^2}
$$

Let $S = (\mu_p - R_B)/\sigma$ be the tangency's excess return per unit of risk over the borrowing rate (which corresponds to the Sharpe ratio in @tbl-tangency) so $\mu_p - R_B = S\sigma$. Substituting, we get

$$
k^* = \frac{S\sigma}{\gamma\,\sigma^2} = \frac{S}{\gamma\,\sigma}
$$

The utility-maximizing portfolio has a $k^*$ weight on (i.e., exposition to) the tangency portfolio and $1 - k^*$ on cash (a negative value here represents borrowing, cf. @tbl-leverage). Its volatility and expected real return are derived as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^* &= k^*\sigma = \frac{S}{\gamma} \\
\mathbb{E}[r] &= R_B + k^*(\mu_p - R_B) = R_B + \frac{S^2}{\gamma}
\end{aligned}
$$

the last step using $k^*(\mu_p - R_B) = \tfrac{S}{\gamma\sigma} \times S\sigma = S^2/\gamma$.

```{python}
#| label: leverage-calc
#| include: false
from leverage import (
    GAMMA,
    levered_allocation,
    levered_expected_return,
    optimal_leverage,
    target_volatility,
)

from mu import BOX_REAL

sh_box = (r_risky - BOX_REAL) / s_risky  # tangency excess over the box borrowing rate
k = optimal_leverage(sh_box, s_risky, GAMMA)
k_fmt = f"{k:.2f}:1"
sstar_fmt = f"{target_volatility(sh_box, GAMMA):.1%}"
erlev_fmt = f"{levered_expected_return(sh_box, GAMMA, rf=BOX_REAL):.1%}"
```

For $\gamma = 2$ we get a leverage ratio of `{python} k_fmt`, a target annualized volatility of `{python} sstar_fmt`, and an expected real return of `{python} erlev_fmt`. @tbl-leverage shows the resulting portfolio.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-leverage
#| tbl-cap: "The tangency portfolio levered to the CRRA optimum (γ = 2), % of NAV."
pd.DataFrame(
    {"% NAV": (levered_allocation(w_risky, k) * 100).round(0).astype(int).astype(str) + " %"}
).rename_axis("position").reset_index().style.hide(axis="index")
```

But that resulting $k^*$ (`{python} k_fmt`) is the unconstrained optimum. Whether margin requirements bring the maximum safe leverage ratio below $k^*$ is what the stress test (@sec-stress) checks.

@tbl-leverage-gamma shows the sensitivity to $\gamma$.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-leverage-gamma
#| tbl-cap: "Leverage, target volatility, and expected real return vs. risk aversion γ."
rows = {}
for g in [1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0]:
    rows[g] = {
        "k* (leverage)": f"{optimal_leverage(sh_box, s_risky, g):.2f}:1",
        "σ* (target vol)": f"{target_volatility(sh_box, g):.1%}",
        "E[r] real": f"{levered_expected_return(sh_box, g, rf=BOX_REAL):.1%}",
    }
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.rename_axis("γ").reset_index().style.hide(axis="index").format(precision=1)
```


# Forced liquidation stress test {#sec-stress}

```{python}
#| label: stress-setup
#| include: false
import stress
from data import daily_returns_matrix

returns_daily = daily_returns_matrix()
daily_start = f"{returns_daily.index.min():%Y-%m}"
daily_f = stress.EURIBOR3M_NOMINAL + 0.003
daily_path = stress.simulate_path(returns_daily, w_risky, k, 0.0, daily_f, 63, periods_per_year=252)
rho0_fmt = f"{1 / k:.1%}"
kstar_fmt = f"{k:.2f}"
daily_min_rho_fmt = f"{daily_path.ratio.min():.1%}"
daily_min_rho_date = f"{daily_path.ratio.idxmin():%Y-%m}"
covid_rho_fmt = f"{daily_path.ratio.loc['2020-02':'2020-04'].min():.1%}"

# One daily bootstrap, reused for the table (@tbl-stress-boot) and the prose below.
_boot = stress.bootstrap_grid(
    returns_daily,
    w_risky,
    k,
    spreads=(0.003,),
    rebalances=stress.DAILY_REBALANCE,
    bootstrap="stationary",
    block=63,
    periods_per_year=252,
    n_paths=2000,
)
_q25 = _boot[
    (_boot["rebalance"] == "quarterly") & (_boot["margin maintenance ratio"] == "25%")
].iloc[0]
pcall25_fmt = _q25["P(liquidation) over 30 y"]
dd_med_fmt = _q25["median drawdown"].lstrip("-")
dd_p5_fmt = _q25["5th percentile drawdown"].lstrip("-")
```

The above leverage ratio's optimality with respect to my risk aversion level is solved. At the same time, the resulting leveraged portfolio also needs to be safe regarding forced liquidation by IBKR. To examine that risk, this section will run the portfolio (i) through our history of returns and (ii) through bootstrapped paths.

A short box spread is a fixed-term, fixed-rate loan. But the borrowed cash is invested in marked-to-market ETFs, and IBKR still liquidates if the account's equity (i.e., NAV) falls below the maintenance margin (even though no margin loan is used). Here's how it works. First the key concepts:

- Gross assets value (GAV, €) = the value of the portfolio's assets, without subtracting liabilities.
- Net asset value (NAV, €) = GAV - liabilities.
- Margin ratio (%) = NAV / GAV. It's the share of the exposure (GAV) that you actually own (NAV), the inverse of the leverage ratio.
- Margin (€) = GAV - NAV.
- Maintenance margin ratio (%) = the margin ratio threshold under which IBKR liquidates some assets to reduce your liabilities and bring your margin ratio above the threshold.
- Maintenance margin (€) = maintenance margin * GAV.
- Excess liquidity (€) = NAV - maintenance margin * GAV.
- Margin cushion (%) = margin ratio - maintenance margin ratio

Liquidation is triggered when your margin ratio falls below the maintenance margin ratio i.e., when the excess liquidity goes negative.

Simulated portfolio mechanics for the stress tests:
- The portfolio starts with a margin ratio $= 1/k =$ `{python} rho0_fmt`.
- I use daily returns. The time range starts on `{python} daily_start`, covering the GFC, the March-2020 crash and the 2022 sell-off.
- I don't apply dynamic, preventive deleveraging between rebalances, so the portfolio's margin ratio decreases after losses.
- I reset the portfolio to the target leverage ratio $k$ and the asset weights quarterly (my plan) or annually (to see the cost of letting more drift occur)
- I finance at the 3-month Euribor plus 0.3 pp (as defined in @sec-leverage).
- We've been speaking in real terms so far but for the stress tests, given that a liquidation is a nominal event, we will speak in nominal terms and the short box spread loan will use a nominal rate rather than the real $R_B$ rate used so far.

IBKR uses "risk-based margin" on European accounts, by default (cf. [here](https://www.interactivebrokers.ie/en/trading/margin-stocks.php?hm=eu&ex=eu&rgt=0&rsk=1&pm=0&rst=040404040404040104) for stocks and [here](https://www.interactivebrokers.ie/en/trading/margin-bonds.php?hm=eu&ex=eu&rgt=0&rsk=1&pm=0&rst=040404040404040104) for bonds). But, in practice, UCITS securities generally carry a 25 % maintenance margin ratio (cf. [this discussion](https://www.reddit.com/r/vosfinances/comments/1vh7lfr/ibkr_maintenance_margin_call/)), so a portfolio made entirely of them should face a 25 % maintenance requirement. But IBKR reserves the right to raise that requirement as it wishes (and it has done so in the past), so we'll also consider two higher levels (30 % & 35 %).


## Historical stress test

@tbl-stress-crisis shows how the portfolio would have behaved, in terms of drawdown & margin ratio, through the crises in our study period. @tbl-stress-hist shows the result of running the portfolio over the whole period for each margin maintenance ratio & rebalancing frequency combination. And @fig-stress plots that result.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-stress-crisis
#| tbl-cap: "The levered portfolio through each crisis: max drawdown and lowest margin ratio reached. Quarterly rebalancing."
stress.crisis_report(
    returns_daily,
    w_risky,
    k,
    daily_f,
    63,
    crises=stress.DAILY_CRISES,
    periods_per_year=252,
).style.hide(axis="index")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-stress-hist
#| tbl-cap: "Full historical simulation: max drawdown, lowest margin cushion, and whether/when a liquidation is triggered."
stress.historical_grid(
    returns_daily,
    w_risky,
    k,
    spreads=(0.003,),
    rebalances=stress.DAILY_REBALANCE,
    periods_per_year=252,
).drop(columns="financing").style.hide(axis="index")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-stress
#| fig-cap: "The levered portfolio over the full daily window (quarterly rebalancing): NAV (top, log scale) and margin ratio (bottom)."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 6), sharex=True, height_ratios=[1.4, 1])

ax1.plot(daily_path.nav.index, daily_path.nav, color="#0072B2", linewidth=1.2)
ax1.set_yscale("log")
ax1.set_ylabel("NAV (log, NAV₀ = 1)")
ax1.grid(True, axis="y", color="0.92")
ax1.set_axisbelow(True)
ax1.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

ax2.plot(daily_path.ratio.index, daily_path.ratio, color="#CC79A7", linewidth=1.0)
for m_line in (0.25, 0.35):
    ax2.axhline(m_line, color="0.5", linewidth=1.0, linestyle=":")
    ax2.text(
        daily_path.ratio.index[20],
        m_line + 0.004,
        f"m = {m_line:.0%}",
        color="0.4",
        fontsize=8,
        va="bottom",
    )
_lo_date = daily_path.ratio.idxmin()
ax2.annotate(
    f"{daily_path.ratio.min():.1%}",
    xy=(_lo_date, daily_path.ratio.min()),
    xytext=(0, -12),
    textcoords="offset points",
    ha="center",
    fontsize=8,
    color="#CC79A7",
)
ax2.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(xmax=1.0))
ax2.set_ylabel("Margin ratio ρ")
_lo = min(daily_path.ratio.min(), 0.25)
_hi = max(daily_path.ratio.max(), 0.35)
_pad = 0.03 * (_hi - _lo)
ax2.set_ylim(_lo - _pad, _hi + _pad)
ax2.grid(True, axis="y", color="0.92")
ax2.set_axisbelow(True)
ax2.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

The historical path never comes down close to the required margin ratio. The margin ratio bottoms at `{python} daily_min_rho_fmt` (`{python} daily_min_rho_date`, the March-2020 crash) -- more than double the 25 % threshold, and with a large cushion even relative to the extreme 35 % threshold (@fig-stress-covid). No threshold is breached anywhere in this realized path (@tbl-stress-hist).


## Bootstrapped stress test

Across 2000 30-year bootstrapped paths (using stationary bootstrapping, cf. Politis & Romano ([1994](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1994.10476870))), no liquidation is ever triggered across the 25 %, 30 %, and 35 % thresholds (@tbl-stress-boot).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-stress-boot
#| tbl-cap: "Results of the stationary-bootstrap (2000 30-year paths, mean block size of ~63 trading days)"
_boot.drop(columns="financing").style.hide(axis="index")
```

So, at the CRRA-optimal $k =$ `{python} kstar_fmt`, the risk of forced liquidation is seems low. Though, this result is regime-dependant, we would need more historical data to make it more robust. And the max drawdown is still substantial, but this is what my personal $\gamma$ accounts for already.
